error_message: syntax error at or near 'last_name'
problem_description: List all customer first and last names.
ground_truth_hint: Take a closer look at your SELECT clause. Are all your column names separated correctly?
reference_answer: You're missing a comma between first_name and last_name in your SELECT clause. Add a comma: SELECT first_name, last_name FROM sales.customers;

student_query: SELECT full_name FROM sales.customers;
error_message: column 'full_name' does not exist
problem_description: List all customer names.
ground_truth_hint: You're referencing a column that doesn't exist in the table. The customers table uses first_name and last_name, not full_name.
reference_answer: The column 'full_name' does not exist in sales.customers. Use first_name and last_name instead.

student_query: SELECT * FROM sales.customer;
error_message: relation 'sales.customer' does not exist
problem_description: Show all customer data.
ground_truth_hint: Look at your FROM clause carefully. Is the table name spelled correctly?
reference_answer: The table name is 'sales.customers' (plural), not 'sales.customer'.

student_query: SELECT o.order_id, c.first_name FROM sales.orders o, sales.customers c;
error_message: missing FROM-clause entry for table
problem_description: List orders with customer first names.
ground_truth_hint:
When combining tables, use an explicit JOIN with an ON condition. Here's a similar example:
SELECT e.name, d.name FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id;
reference_answer: Use JOIN with ON: SELECT o.order_id, c.first_name FROM sales.orders o JOIN sales.customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;

student_query: SELECT store_id, product_name, COUNT(*) FROM production.products GROUP BY store_id;
error_message: column 'product_name' must appear in GROUP BY clause or aggregate
problem_description: Count products per store.
ground_truth_hint: You have a GROUP BY error. Every column in SELECT must either appear in GROUP BY or be wrapped in an aggregate function.
reference_answer: Remove product_name from SELECT or add it to GROUP BY. Since you want a count per store, just SELECT store_id, COUNT(*).

student_query: SELECT * FROM sales.orders WHERE customer_id = (SELECT customer_id FROM sales.customers WHERE state = 'NY');
error_message: more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression
problem_description: Find orders from New York customers.
ground_truth_hint: When a subquery can return multiple rows, use IN instead of =. Example: WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM table WHERE condition);
reference_answer: Use IN instead of =: WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM sales.customers WHERE state = 'NY');

reference_answer: list_price is a numeric column. Use a number instead of a string: WHERE list_price > 1000;

error_message: Query runs but returns wrong results. Expected customers who placed orders.

Here's a template to help:
SELECT ___
FROM sales.customers c
JOIN ___ ON ___

student_query: SELECT order_id, first_name FROM sales.orders JOIN sales.customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.customer_id;
error_message: column reference 'order_id' is ambiguous
problem_description: List orders with customer names.
ground_truth_hint: You have an ambiguous column reference. When joining tables that share column names, prefix each column with the table name or alias.
reference_answer: Use table aliases: SELECT o.order_id, c.first_name FROM sales.orders o JOIN sales.customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;

student_query: SELECT * FROM sales.orders, production.products;
error_message: statement timeout — query exceeded time limit
problem_description: List orders with product details.
ground_truth_hint: Your query timed out — it's too slow. This is usually a Cartesian product: a missing JOIN condition causing every row in one table to pair with every row in another. Check that each table in your FROM clause has a matching ON condition.
reference_answer: Add proper JOINs: FROM sales.orders o JOIN sales.order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN production.products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id;

student_query: SELECT p.product_name, b.brand_name FROM production.products p JOIN production.brands b ON p.product_id = b.brand_id;
error_message: Wrong results — join key mismatch

reference_answer: Use the correct FK: JOIN production.brands b ON p.brand_id = b.brand_id;

student_query: SELECT category_id, AVG(list_price) FROM production.products WHERE AVG(list_price) > 500 GROUP BY category_id;
error_message: aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE
problem_description: Find categories with average price above $500.
ground_truth_hint:
Aggregate functions like AVG() cannot be used in WHERE. Example:
SELECT dept, AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000;
reference_answer: Use HAVING instead of WHERE for aggregate conditions: HAVING AVG(list_price) > 500;

student_query: SELECT product_name, list_price FROM production.products WHERE list_price > 0;
error_message: Query runs but returns too many rows. Expected only products with orders.
problem_description: List products that have been ordered at least once.
ground_truth_hint: Your query returns all products, but the problem asks only for products that have been ordered. Think about which table tracks orders.
reference_answer: Add a subquery or JOIN to filter for ordered products: WHERE product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM sales.order_items);

student_query: SELECT product_name list_price FROM production.products;
error_message: syntax error at or near "list_price"
problem_description: List each product's name and price.

reference_answer: Missing comma: SELECT product_name, list_price FROM production.products;

problem_description: List the price of every product.

reference_answer: The column is list_price, not product_price: SELECT list_price FROM production.products;

error_message: invalid input syntax for type integer: "new"
problem_description: Find products from the newest model year available.

reference_answer: Compare against a year number, e.g. WHERE model_year = 2019, or use MAX(model_year).

student_query: SELECT category_id FROM production.products;

Your query is technically correct but doesn't collapse repeats. Here's the general pattern for keeping only unique rows:
SELECT DISTINCT col FROM table;
reference_answer: Add DISTINCT: SELECT DISTINCT category_id FROM production.products;

student_query: SELECT product_name, list_price FROM production.products ORDER BY list_price;
error_message: Query runs but sorts cheapest-first; expected most expensive first.
problem_description: List products from most to least expensive.
ground_truth_hint: Look at your ORDER BY clause — by default it sorts ascending. Is that what the problem asked for?
reference_answer: Add DESC: ORDER BY list_price DESC;

student_query: SELECT o.order_id, s.store_name FROM sales.orders o, sales.stores s;
error_message: Query runs but returns far more rows than orders exist (Cartesian product).
problem_description: List each order with the name of the store it was placed at.
ground_truth_hint: Listing two tables with a comma and no condition pairs every row with every row. You need an explicit JOIN with a matching condition.
reference_answer: SELECT o.order_id, s.store_name FROM sales.orders o JOIN sales.stores s ON o.store_id = s.store_id;

student_query: SELECT p.product_name, c.category_name FROM production.products p NATURAL JOIN production.categories c;
error_message: Query runs but returns unexpected/incorrect results.
problem_description: List each product with its category name.
ground_truth_hint:
NATURAL JOIN matches on every column the two tables share by name, which isn't always what you want. Here's a similar example using an explicit condition instead:
SELECT e.name, d.name FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id;
reference_answer: Use an explicit ON clause: JOIN production.categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id;

student_query: SELECT s.first_name, s.manager_id FROM sales.staffs s;
error_message: Query runs but shows a manager_id number, not the manager's name.
problem_description: List each staff member together with their manager's name.
ground_truth_hint:
Here's a template — you need to join the staffs table to itself:
SELECT s.first_name, ___.first_name AS manager_name
FROM sales.staffs s
JOIN sales.staffs ___ ON s.manager_id = ___.staff_id;
reference_answer: SELECT s.first_name, m.first_name AS manager_name FROM sales.staffs s JOIN sales.staffs m ON s.manager_id = m.staff_id;

error_message: column reference "customer_id" is ambiguous
problem_description: List the customer and product for every order line.

reference_answer: Qualify it: SELECT o.customer_id, p.product_name FROM sales.orders o JOIN sales.order_items oi USING (order_id) JOIN production.products p USING (product_id);

error_message: column "staff_id" specified in USING clause does not exist in right table
problem_description: List each order with the name of the store it was placed at.

student_query: SELECT c.first_name, o.order_id FROM sales.customers c JOIN sales.orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
error_message: Query runs but omits customers who have never placed an order.
problem_description: List every customer and their orders, including customers who haven't ordered yet.
ground_truth_hint: A plain JOIN only keeps rows that match on both sides. You need an outer join to keep customers with no matching order too.
reference_answer: SELECT c.first_name, o.order_id FROM sales.customers c LEFT JOIN sales.orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

student_query: SELECT p.product_name, s.quantity FROM production.stocks s LEFT JOIN production.products p ON s.product_id = p.product_id;
error_message: Query runs but drops products with no stock row recorded.
problem_description: List every product and its stock quantity, including products with no stock recorded.
ground_truth_hint:
A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the *left* table. You wrote stocks on the left, but you want every product kept — even ones with no stock. Here's the pattern:
SELECT a.x, b.y FROM b LEFT JOIN a ON ...  -- 'a' is the side you keep in full
reference_answer: SELECT p.product_name, s.quantity FROM production.products p LEFT JOIN production.stocks s ON s.product_id = p.product_id;

student_query: SELECT c.first_name, o.order_id FROM sales.customers c LEFT JOIN sales.orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
error_message: Query runs but only surfaces unmatched customers, not any orphaned orders.
problem_description: Find any customers with no order, and any orders with no matching customer, in one result.
ground_truth_hint:
Here's a template — you need unmatched rows from *both* sides at once:
SELECT c.first_name, o.order_id
FROM sales.customers c
___ JOIN sales.orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
reference_answer: SELECT c.first_name, o.order_id FROM sales.customers c FULL OUTER JOIN sales.orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

student_query: SELECT c.customer_id FROM sales.customers c LEFT JOIN sales.orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_id = 5;
error_message: Query runs but doesn't find customers with no orders.
problem_description: Find customers who have never placed an order.
ground_truth_hint: Think about what an unmatched row looks like after an outer join. What value would o.order_id hold for a customer with no orders?
reference_answer: SELECT c.customer_id FROM sales.customers c LEFT JOIN sales.orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;

student_query: SELECT c.first_name, o.order_id FROM sales.customers c LEFT JOIN sales.orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_status = 4;
error_message: Query runs but drops customers with no completed order — behaves like an inner join.
problem_description: List every customer, and their completed orders (status 4) if any — customers without one should still appear.
ground_truth_hint: A condition on the outer table in WHERE runs *after* the join and silently discards the unmatched rows you just kept. Move that condition into the ON clause instead.
reference_answer: SELECT c.first_name, o.order_id FROM sales.customers c LEFT JOIN sales.orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.order_status = 4;

ground_truth_hint: Every non-aggregated column in SELECT has to appear in GROUP BY too. Which column here isn't in either place?
reference_answer: Either add brand_name to GROUP BY, or drop it: SELECT category_id, COUNT(*) FROM production.products GROUP BY category_id;

student_query: SELECT store_id, COUNT(shipped_date) FROM sales.orders GROUP BY store_id;

reference_answer: Use COUNT(*) instead: SELECT store_id, COUNT(*) FROM sales.orders GROUP BY store_id;

student_query: SELECT staff_id FROM sales.orders WHERE COUNT(*) > 10 GROUP BY staff_id;
error_message: aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE
problem_description: Find staff who have handled more than 10 orders.
ground_truth_hint:
WHERE filters rows before grouping, so it can't see an aggregate result yet. Here's the pattern for filtering on a group's aggregate:
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
reference_answer: SELECT staff_id FROM sales.orders GROUP BY staff_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;

ground_truth_hint: Look at your GROUP BY clause — how many columns are in it, and does the problem actually need that many?

student_query: SELECT product_name, (SELECT quantity FROM production.stocks WHERE product_id = p.product_id) AS qty FROM production.products p;
error_message: more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression
problem_description: List each product with its stock quantity.

reference_answer: Aggregate it, or join instead: (SELECT SUM(quantity) FROM production.stocks WHERE product_id = p.product_id) AS qty

student_query: SELECT product_name FROM production.products p WHERE list_price > (SELECT AVG(list_price) FROM production.products WHERE category_id = category_id);
error_message: Query runs but returns wrong results — every row compares against the overall average, not its own category's.
problem_description: Find products priced above the average price within their own category.
ground_truth_hint: Your subquery's category_id compares to itself, so it always matches every row — it never actually looks at the outer product's category. A correlated subquery needs to reference the outer table's alias explicitly.
reference_answer: WHERE list_price > (SELECT AVG(list_price) FROM production.products p2 WHERE p2.category_id = p.category_id)

student_query: SELECT product_name, list_price FROM production.products WHERE list_price > ANY (SELECT list_price FROM production.products WHERE category_id = 3);
error_message: Query runs but returns far more products than expected.
problem_description: Find products priced higher than every product in category 3.
ground_truth_hint: ANY only requires beating the smallest value the subquery returns. Which keyword means 'beats every value'?
reference_answer: Use ALL instead: WHERE list_price > ALL (SELECT list_price FROM production.products WHERE category_id = 3);

student_query: SELECT category_id, AVG(list_price) FROM production.products GROUP BY category_id HAVING AVG(list_price) > (SELECT list_price FROM production.products);
error_message: more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression
problem_description: Find categories whose average price is above the overall average product price.
ground_truth_hint: Your subquery in HAVING returns one price per product — not a single overall value. What aggregate would collapse it to one number?
reference_answer: HAVING AVG(list_price) > (SELECT AVG(list_price) FROM production.products)
